newsitem.title: USA: Portugal committed to EMU in 1999-finance minister.
newsitem.headline: Portugal committed to EMU in 1999-finance minister.

text.p: Portugal is committed to joining European monetary union at its launch in 1999 and expects to meet the criteria for membership, Finance Minister Antonio de Sousa Franco said on Wednesday.

"My country's commitment to the single currency in 1999, according to the calendar and convergence criteria, is as strong as our commitment to Europe," he told the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.

"Portugal is fully committee to monetary union and has adopted convergence policies and measures to fulfil in 1997 the conditions for participating in the third phase of EMU," he said, reiterating a previous pledge to be ready for EMU.
Portugal planned to cut its budget deficit to 4.1 percent of gross domestic product this year and 2.9 percent in 1997 from 6.9 percent in 1993.
Debt was expected to fall to 70.7 percent of GDP this year from 71.5 percent in 1995.
"As a result of acceleration of the privatisation programme and improved debt management, this ratio should fall again next year," he added.
Under the Maastricht treaty on monetary union, deficits must be reduced to three percent of GDP and debt lowered towards 60 percent of GDP by next year.

"The current upturn in major European economies should provide further stimuli to our growth, improving conditions for further reducing fiscal deficits. We expect for 1997 a three percent growth, higher than that of 1996," he said.
The inflation rate -- another Maastricht treaty criterion -- at 3.3. percent, was 0.8 percentage points above the EU average.
"The 1997 objective is a further decline in inflation, bringing the rate to between 2 1/4 and 2 1/2 percent," he said.

Ten-year interest rates, also covered by the treaty, were now less than two percentage points above the equivalent German rates, compared to more than four percentage points last year, while the escudo had been stable in the last few years.
